Heart Failure

On this page
A clinical syndrome where the heart can't deliver enough output (or can only do so at the cost of high filling pressures) — corroborated by elevated natriuretic peptides and/or objective congestion.
HFrEF ≤40% · HFmrEF 41–49% · HFpEF ≥50% 4 pillars: ARNI · β-blocker · MRA · SGLT2i NT-proBNP rules it out if low Norepinephrine = 1st-line shock pressor
Shared

Pathophysiology & classification

🧬

The neurohormonal vicious cycle

Whatever the index insult — a big MI, years of hypertension, a leaky valve, a cardiomyopathy — the common endpoint is a heart that can no longer move enough blood forward. The body senses the drop in effective arterial blood volume exactly the way it would sense hemorrhage, and it turns on the same two ancient rescue systems: the sympathetic nervous system and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS). Over minutes to hours those systems are lifesaving. Over months they are the disease.

a driver flooring the gas pedal because the engine is losing power. More throttle (adrenaline, angiotensin) does buy a little speed — but you're redlining an already-failing engine, burning it out faster. Every drug that helps heart failure is essentially a foot easing off that pedal.
  1. Sympathetic activation: norepinephrine raises heart rate, contractility, and systemic vasoconstriction. Chronic exposure is directly toxic to myocytes (apoptosis), downregulates β-receptors, and is arrhythmogenic.
  2. RAAS activation: renal hypoperfusion → renin → angiotensin II (potent vasoconstriction → ↑afterload) → aldosterone (Na⁺/water retention → ↑preload, plus direct myocardial and vascular fibrosis).
  3. Natriuretic peptides (ANP/BNP) are the counter-regulatory "good" hormones released by stretched myocardium — they promote natriuresis, vasodilation, and are anti-fibrotic. In HF they're overwhelmed, and they get chewed up by the enzyme neprilysin (which is exactly why we inhibit neprilysin with ARNI).
  4. Remodeling: chamber dilation and eccentric hypertrophy raise wall stress (Laplace: stress ∝ pressure × radius), worsen mitral regurgitation, and feed the spiral forward.
The self-perpetuating spiral of heart failure. Each guideline drug class interrupts a specific limb — that mapping is the through-line of this whole guide.
because the four GDMT pillars each cut a different wire in this circuit: β-blockers silence the toxic sympathetic drive, ACEi/ARB/ARNI and MRA shut down RAAS-driven afterload and fibrosis, ARNI additionally preserves the protective natriuretic peptides by blocking neprilysin, and SGLT2i unload volume and improve cardiac energetics. Fixing the pump you can't; interrupting the maladaptive response you can — and that's what improves survival.
📉

Frank–Starling: why more fluid stops helping

A normal ventricle sits on the steep part of the Starling curve — give it more preload and stroke volume rises. The failing ventricle operates on a flattened curve: extra volume no longer buys output, it just backs up as filling pressure → pulmonary congestion. GDMT (and afterload reduction) shifts the whole curve up and to the left, so the heart does more work at a lower, safer filling pressure.

On the flat HFrEF curve, loading fluid raises pressure without raising output — that's decompensation. Therapy lifts the curve so the same output happens at lower filling pressure.

Classification — the vocabulary you'll use on rounds

By ejection fraction (2021 Universal Definition)

CategoryLVEFWhat drives it & what works
HFrEF (reduced)≤40%Systolic/neurohormonal — the 4 pillars all have mortality benefit.
HFmrEF (mildly reduced)41–49%Overlap phenotype; SGLT2i + treat like HFrEF-lite.
HFpEF (preserved)≥50%Diastolic stiffness/inflammation; SGLT2i is the anchor.
HFimpEF (improved)Was ≤40%, now >40% +≥10 ptsContinue GDMT indefinitely — stopping it relapses (TRED-HF).

NYHA class (symptoms — can change day to day)

  • I — no limitation
  • II — symptoms with ordinary activity
  • III — symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity
  • IV — symptoms at rest

ACC/AHA stage (structural — only moves forward)

  • A — at risk (HTN, DM, CAD), no structural disease
  • B — structural disease, no symptoms (pre-HF)
  • C — structural disease + symptoms
  • D — advanced/refractory; transplant/LVAD/inotrope/hospice
NYHA is reversible (a patient can go from III back to II with diuresis); ACC/AHA stage is a ratchet that only advances. Use NYHA to track response, stage to frame the big picture.
🏛️

The four pillars — each blocks one arm of the cascade

Modern GDMT = get all four pillars on board early, then up-titrate — low-dose quadruple therapy beats high-dose partial therapy.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Every finding in heart failure traces back to one of two problems: backward failure (blood damming behind the failing chamber → congestion) or forward failure (not enough output → hypoperfusion). Read each sign as a clue to which is dominant.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Exertional dyspnea~90%↑LA pressure → pulmonary capillary congestion → stiff, wet lungs + J-receptor stimulation. The earliest, most sensitive symptom.
Fatigue / exercise intolerance~80%Low forward output → skeletal-muscle hypoperfusion, impaired O₂ delivery, deconditioning.
Crackles (rales)~60–70%Transudation of fluid into alveoli/interstitium. May be absent in chronic HF as lymphatics adapt.
Orthopnea~50–70%Lying flat shifts splanchnic/leg venous blood centrally → ↑pulmonary pressures within minutes.
Peripheral edema~50–65%↑systemic venous pressure + RAAS-driven Na⁺/water retention → gravity-dependent capillary transudation.
PND (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea)~40%Nighttime reabsorption of interstitial edema + reduced respiratory drive in sleep → wakes gasping after 1–2 h.
Elevated JVP~40%A direct window on right-atrial/central venous pressure — the best bedside congestion marker (specific).
S3 gallop~15–30%Rapid early-diastolic filling into a volume-loaded, compliance-limited ventricle — highly specific for ↑filling pressure.
Hepatomegaly / RUQ fullness~15–25%Hepatic venous congestion ("nutmeg liver") from elevated right-heart pressures.
Cool extremities / narrow pulse pressure<15%The "cold" low-output profile — peripheral vasoconstriction to defend BP; flags impending cardiogenic shock.
Ascites<15%Chronic severe systemic venous congestion, usually biventricular/right-heart failure.
Read the patternCongestion signs (JVD, S3, orthopnea, edema) say they're wet; low-output signs (cool, narrow pulse pressure, oliguria, hyponatremia) say they're cold. That wet/cold read is the Stevenson profile that drives your whole plan.
🪛

Imaging findings — and the order they appear

CXR findingWhen it appearsWhy
Cephalization (upper-lobe vascular redistribution)Earliest (PCWP ~13–18)Rising pulmonary venous pressure recruits upper-lobe vessels normally collapsed when upright.
Kerley B linesPCWP ~18–25Fluid in the interlobular septa — interstitial edema.
Perihilar "bat-wing" alveolar edemaPCWP >25Alveolar flooding once interstitial capacity is exceeded.
Pleural effusions (R > L)CommonElevated systemic + pulmonary venous pressure; right-sided predominance.
Cardiomegaly (CTR >0.5)Chronic HFrEFChamber dilation/eccentric remodeling; often absent in acute HFpEF or flash edema.
Radiographic congestion lags the hemodynamics by hours, and up to ~20% of acute HF patients have a near-normal CXR — a clear film does not rule out ADHF. Correlate with exam, POCUS B-lines, and natriuretic peptides.
🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you

LabWhat it means & why it moves
NT-proBNP / BNPReleased when ventricular myocytes are stretched (wall tension), so it tracks filling pressure. Rules HF out when low (BNP <100 / NT-proBNP <300). Falsely high with age, renal dysfunction, AF, RV strain/PE, sepsis; falsely low with obesity. BNP is a neprilysin substrate → ARNI raises BNP but not NT-proBNP, so follow NT-proBNP on sacubitril/valsartan.
SodiumHyponatremia = neurohormonal water retention (non-osmotic ADH release from low output) → a marker of severity and worse prognosis, not just "too much water."
Creatinine / BUNCardiorenal syndrome: venous congestion (high renal venous pressure) impairs GFR as much as low forward flow does. A high BUN:Cr ratio signals prerenal/RAAS activation. A transient ↑Cr from hemoconcentration during effective diuresis can be benign.
TroponinMild elevation is common from subendocardial demand/strain in ADHF; a large or rising level points to ACS as the precipitant.
LactateElevated = tissue hypoperfusion — the biochemical signature of the "cold"/shock patient; clearance tracks resuscitation.
LFTs / bilirubinChronic congestion → ↑alk phos/bilirubin (congestive hepatopathy); a sharp AST/ALT spike in shock = ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver").
Potassium / magnesiumLoop diuretics waste both (arrhythmia risk) while RAAS/MRA drive hyperkalemia — the daily inpatient balancing act.

Assess

Recognizing chronic HF

🔍

How it presents outpatient

Clinic HF is usually the slow burn: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, and lower-extremity edema, often with gradually falling exercise tolerance and rising weight. The most specific findings are an S3 gallop and elevated JVP; the most sensitive symptom is exertional dyspnea.

FindingWhat it tells you
Orthopnea / PNDRedistribution of fluid when supine → elevated LA pressure.
Elevated JVP, hepatojugular refluxBest bedside marker of volume/right-sided filling pressure.
S3 gallopRapid early filling into a stiff/volume-loaded LV — specific for HF.
Bibasilar crackles, edemaPresent but nonspecific; absence does not exclude chronic HF (lymphatics compensate).
In chronic compensated HF the lungs can be dry despite high filling pressures because pulmonary lymphatics adapt — trust the JVP and weight trend over crackles.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Initial outpatient workup

NT-proBNP / BNPFirst test when HF is suspected. Elevated supports the diagnosis and gives a baseline to trend. Low value has high negative predictive value.First
Echocardiogram (TTE)The pivotal test — gives EF (phenotype), wall motion, valves, filling pressures, RV. Order in every new HF diagnosis.First
ECGIschemia, prior MI (Q waves), LVH, AF, QRS width (matters for future CRT).First
BMP, CBC, LFTs, TSHBaseline renal function/K⁺ before RAAS/MRA; anemia and thyroid disease as precipitants/mimics; congestive hepatopathy.First
Iron studies (ferritin, TSAT)Iron deficiency is common and treatable even without anemia (ferritin <100, or 100–299 with TSAT <20%).First
Fasting lipids, HbA1cRisk-factor and comorbidity management (statin, SGLT2i for DM).First
Ischemic evaluationWhen: new HFrEF, angina, or regional wall-motion abnormality → stress test or coronary angiography to find reversible ischemic cause.If indicated
New HFrEF with no obvious cause → look for a reversible etiology before calling it idiopathic: ischemia (angiogram), tachycardia-mediated (rate-control AF), valvular, thyroid, iron overload, and toxins (alcohol, chemo, methamphetamine).

3
Devices & advanced referral
Reassess EF after ≥3 months of GDMT first
▾
  • ICD (primary prevention): LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II–III on GDMT ≥3 months, survival >1 yr; ischemic cardiomyopathy also qualifies at LVEF ≤30%. Wait ≥40 days post-MI and ≥90 days on GDMT before reassessing EF — many recover.
  • CRT (biventricular pacing): LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms, NYHA II–IV on GDMT (strongest benefit). Weaker for non-LBBB or QRS 120–149 ms.
  • Advanced (Stage D) referral: refractory symptoms, recurrent admissions, inotrope dependence, low output → transplant / LVAD / palliative evaluation.
Don't implant a primary-prevention ICD on the first low EF. Optimize GDMT for 3 months and re-echo — a large fraction of EFs recover past the 35% threshold and no longer need the device.
🫙

HFpEF (EF ≥50%) — different disease, different playbook

Here the lesion is a stiff, non-compliant ventricle driven by comorbidity-related inflammation (HTN, obesity, DM, CKD, aging), not systolic neurohormonal remodeling — which is exactly why most HFrEF drugs failed in HFpEF trials.

TherapyDoseEvidenceRole
SGLT2i (dapa/empa)10 mg daily (no titration)EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVERClass 1 anchor — the one class that works across the whole EF spectrum.
Finerenone (nonsteroidal MRA)Start 10 mg daily (eGFR 25–<60) or 20 mg (eGFR ≥60); target 20 mg dailyFINEARTS-HF (2024)Emerging second pillar; ↓HF events even on top of SGLT2i.
Spironolactone12.5–25 → 25–50 mg daily (same K⁺/eGFR gate)TOPCAT (Americas subgroup)Reasonable, esp. EF closer to 50% with elevated NP.
Loop diuretic + BP control + comorbidity mgmtLoop titrated to euvolemia; BP <130/80Class 1Treat congestion, hypertension, AF, obesity, sleep apnea, CKD aggressively.
HFrEF is a weak pump; HFpEF is a stiff balloon. You can't squeeze harder into a stiff balloon — you manage what fills it (volume, BP, heart rate, atrial kick) and the SGLT2i that helps regardless.
Monitor

Titration & follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • After starting/uptitrating ACEi/ARB/ARNI or MRA: BMP (K⁺, Cr) at 1–2 weeks; for MRA also ~day 3 and day 7, then periodically.
  • SGLT2i: expect a small initial eGFR dip (reversible) — don't stop for it; monitor volume status.
  • Home weights daily — teach the patient to call for a gain of >2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week.
  • NT-proBNP trend and re-echo for EF reassessment (especially before ICD/CRT decisions after ≥3 months of GDMT).
  • STRONG-HF model: after a hospitalization, up-titrate to full GDMT within ~2 weeks with labs/exam at weeks 1, 2, 3, 6 — the highest-yield way to prevent readmission.
Once a patient is on sacubitril/valsartan, follow NT-proBNP, not BNP. Neprilysin inhibition raises BNP (a neprilysin substrate) but not NT-proBNP, so BNP looks falsely worse on ARNI.
Comorbidities

How comorbidities change HF management

🔗

The company heart failure keeps

Heart failure almost never travels alone, and each companion disease bends the plan. Manage the pair, not the pump in isolation.

ComorbidityHow it interactsWhat changes
CKD / cardiorenalVenous congestion drops GFR; RAAS/MRA raise K⁺; diuretic resistance.Respect eGFR gates, watch K⁺, use K-binders; SGLT2i still beneficial and renoprotective; avoid NSAIDs/contrast; sequential nephron blockade for resistance.
Atrial fibrillationLoss of atrial kick + tachycardia worsens filling (esp. HFpEF); can cause tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.Rate control with β-blocker ± digoxin (avoid verapamil/diltiazem in HFrEF); anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; consider ablation (CASTLE-AF).
Type 2 diabetesAccelerates CAD and remodeling.Prefer SGLT2i (dual benefit); metformin safe; avoid thiazolidinediones (fluid) and saxagliptin (↑HF hospitalization).
COPD / asthmaOverlapping dyspnea; reflex fear of β-blockers.Don't withhold a cardioselective β-blocker — use bisoprolol or metoprolol (β1-selective); generally well tolerated.
CAD / ischemiaMost common cause of HFrEF; ongoing ischemia depresses function.Revascularize significant ischemia; statin; treat angina (nitrates, β-blocker).
HypertensionAfterload driver; leading cause of HFpEF.Target <130/80; several GDMT agents double as antihypertensives.
Iron deficiency (± anemia)Worsens symptoms/functional capacity independent of hemoglobin.IV iron if ferritin <100, or 100–299 with TSAT <20%; oral iron doesn't work.
Sleep-disordered breathingOSA worsens afterload/arrhythmia; central sleep apnea marks severity.Treat OSA (CPAP); avoid adaptive servo-ventilation in HFrEF with central sleep apnea (SERVE-HF ↑mortality).
ObesityMajor HFpEF driver (inflammation, plasma volume expansion).Weight loss; SGLT2i; GLP-1 agonists emerging for the HFpEF-obesity phenotype.
Avoid / use caution in HFrEF: NSAIDs (Na⁺ retention, blunt diuretics, worsen renal), non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem — negative inotropes), thiazolidinediones (fluid), saxagliptin/alogliptin (↑HF hospitalization), most class I & III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone and dofetilide are the safe ones), and high-dose corticosteroids.
Scores

Risk calculators

🧮

CHA₂DS₂-VASc — stroke risk in AF (do they need anticoagulation?)

Most HF patients already score ≥1 — heart failure itself is the "C". Use it whenever HF coexists with atrial fibrillation to decide on anticoagulation.

Congestive HF / LV dysfunction +1
Hypertension +1
Diabetes +1
Prior stroke / TIA / thromboembolism +2
Vascular disease (MI, PAD, aortic plaque) +1
Female sex +1
Age (pick one)
<65 years 0
65–74 years +1
≥75 years +2
1
Anticoagulate (DOAC preferred over warfarin unless mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis) at ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women. A score of 1 (men) / 2 (women) is a "consider" zone; a female-sex-only score of 1 does not by itself warrant anticoagulation.
🩸

HAS-BLED — bleeding risk (weigh against the stroke benefit)

Uncontrolled hypertension (SBP >160) +1
Abnormal renal function (dialysis, transplant, Cr >2.26) +1
Abnormal liver function (cirrhosis; bili >2× + AST/ALT >3×) +1
Prior stroke +1
Prior major bleed / predisposition +1
Labile INR (TTR <60%) +1
Elderly (age >65) +1
Drugs — antiplatelet / NSAID +1
Alcohol ≥8 drinks/week +1
0
A high HAS-BLED (≥3) is a flag to correct modifiable bleeding risks (BP, labile INR, alcohol, unnecessary antiplatelets/NSAIDs) and follow more closely — not a reason to withhold anticoagulation when the stroke risk warrants it.

GradeRecommendationPopulation

Vaccinate & manage comorbidities (each reduces HF events)

  • Vaccines: annual influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, RSV (age-appropriate) — Class 1.
  • AF: rate/rhythm control + anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; ablation reasonable in HFrEF+AF (CASTLE-AF).
  • HTN target <130/80; DM prefer SGLT2i (dual benefit); CKD SGLT2i/finerenone.
  • Sleep apnea: treat OSA — but avoid adaptive servo-ventilation in HFrEF with central sleep apnea (SERVE-HF: ↑mortality).
  • Iron deficiency: IV iron (not oral).
Escalate

When clinic isn't enough

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Rest dyspnea or hypoxia / frank pulmonary edema · hypotension with hypoperfusion (cool, confused, oliguric — think cardiogenic shock) · chest pain or suspected ACS · syncope or sustained symptomatic arrhythmia · rapid weight gain with refractory congestion despite oral diuretic uptitration · symptomatic hyponatremia, severe hyper/hypokalemia, or acute kidney injury.

Admit

Who to admit & how to profile them

📋

Precipitant + hemodynamic profile

First ask why now? — decompensation almost always has a trigger. Mnemonic "FAILURE": Forgot meds/diet, Arrhythmia (AF/RVR)/Anemia, Ischemia/Infection, Lifestyle (Na/fluid), Upregulation (thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy), Renal failure, Embolism (PE). Also NSAIDs, non-dihydropyridine CCBs, uncontrolled HTN.

Then classify by the two questions that drive every management decision: Is the patient congested (wet/dry)? Is the patient perfused (warm/cold)?

Stevenson profiles. Wet = JVD, rales, edema, orthopnea, S3. Cold = narrow pulse pressure, cool extremities, ↓urine, hyponatremia, rising Cr. Try the interactive selector below.

Treat

Acute management — decongest first

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy

1
IV loop diuresis (the workhorse for "wet")
Dose ≈ 2.5× total daily oral home dose
▾
oral diuretic absorption is erratic when the gut wall is edematous, and the failing kidney needs a bigger push to reach the loop of Henle. IV delivery + a higher dose overcomes both.
  • DOSE trial: bolus and continuous infusion are equivalent; high-dose (2.5× total daily oral, IV) beat low-dose for decongestion with only transient reversible ↑Cr. Give IV furosemide ≈ 2.5× the home oral total, q12h, then titrate to urine output and weight.
  • Diuretic resistance? Add a thiazide (metolazone 2.5–10 mg PO or IV chlorothiazide 500 mg) 30 min before the loop for sequential nephron blockade — watch K⁺/Mg²⁺ closely.
  • Ultrafiltration: reserve for truly diuretic-refractory congestion (CARRESS-HF showed no renal advantage over stepped pharmacologic care).
A transient bump in creatinine during effective decongestion is acceptable — don't reflexively stop diuresing a still-congested, otherwise-stable patient. "Worsening renal function" that's really just hemoconcentration predicts better outcomes.
2
Vasodilators — for hypertensive / flash pulmonary edema
SCAPE physiology
▾
  • IV nitroglycerin (start ~10–20 mcg/min, titrate up): preload and afterload reduction — the key drug in hypertensive acute pulmonary edema (SCAPE) and ongoing ischemia. In SCAPE the problem is afterload/redistribution more than total-body fluid, so vasodilation works faster than diuresis.
  • Nitroprusside: potent balanced vasodilator for severe HTN or acute valvular regurgitation; needs an arterial line; watch cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity and coronary steal.
3
Continue vs hold GDMT during the admission
The instinct to "hold everything" is usually wrong
▾
  • β-blocker: continue unless overtly cold/hypoperfused or in shock — abrupt withdrawal worsens outcomes (B-CONVINCED). Reduce the dose rather than stop. Do not start a β-blocker in a wet, unstable patient — wait until euvolemic.
  • ACEi/ARB/ARNI: continue unless hypotension, AKI, or hyperkalemia.
  • SGLT2i: hold if euglycemic-DKA risk (NPO, sepsis); otherwise increasingly continued/initiated in-hospital.
  • Initiate/optimize GDMT before discharge (Class 1) — the hospitalization is the single highest-yield window to get pillars on board.
4
"Cold" patient — low output
This is where the floor starts calling the ICU
▾

A cold/hypoperfused patient (narrow pulse pressure, cool, oliguric, rising lactate/Cr) has crossed from a diuresis problem into an output problem. Diuretics alone won't fix perfusion — these patients need inotropic support and belong in a monitored setting. See the ICU context for pressors/inotropes.

Cold + wet + hypotensive = cardiogenic shock physiology. Don't keep pushing diuretics into a hypoperfused patient — call the ICU, start thinking inotrope, and get invasive monitoring.
Diuretics

Loop diuretics — pick the agent & the dose

💧

Which loop, what starting dose, what to watch

loop diuretics block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb — the nephron's biggest sodium-reabsorption site — producing brisk natriuresis plus secondary venodilation that drops preload quickly.

Starting dose

  • Already on a home loop: give at least the total daily oral dose as a single IV dose, up to 2.5× the total daily oral dose IV for aggressive decongestion (DOSE), split q12h, then titrate to urine output/weight.
  • Loop-naïve or home dose unknown: start furosemide 20–40 mg IV (40 mg with any renal impairment). Reassess the urine response over ~2 h and double the dose if inadequate rather than repeating the same dose.
  • Good early response: >100–150 mL urine in the first 1–2 h after an IV dose; aim net negative ~1–2 L/day until euvolemic.

The three loops — and when to use which

AgentPO→IVEquivalenceOral bioavailability / durationWhen to use
Furosemide (Lasix)2:1 (40 PO ≈ 20 IV)40 mg reference~10–100% (erratic, worse with gut edema); short — dose BID–TIDDefault — cheap, familiar, easy to titrate IV in hospital.
Bumetanide (Bumex)~1:11 mg ≈ 40 mg furosemide~80–100% (predictable); shortWhen oral furosemide absorption is unreliable / high doses needed.
Torsemide (Demadex)~1:120 mg ≈ 40 mg furosemide~80–100% (most reliable); long — once dailyBest for reliable outpatient control and gut-edema poor responders; possible anti-fibrotic effect. TRANSFORM-HF: no mortality difference vs furosemide.
Poor response to oral furosemide at home, or gut edema on the floor → switch to torsemide or bumetanide for their reliable absorption before calling it "diuretic resistance." True resistance → add a thiazide (metolazone 2.5–10 mg ~30 min before the loop) for sequential nephron blockade.

Side effects & what to monitor when you start

Watch forWhy / what to do
Hypokalemia & hypomagnesemiaDistal K⁺/Mg²⁺ wasting → arrhythmia. Check BMP + Mg daily; replete (K⁺ >4, Mg²⁺ >2). MRAs and K⁺ supplements offset this.
HyponatremiaFree-water retention; worsens with over-diuresis + thiazide. Marker of severity.
Contraction (metabolic) alkalosisVolume/chloride loss; can blunt further diuresis — sometimes needs KCl or acetazolamide.
Prerenal AKI / over-diuresisTrend Cr; a modest rise during decongestion is acceptable, a steep rise with hypotension is not.
OtotoxicityHigh-dose or rapid IV push (esp. with aminoglycosides) — infuse large IV doses slowly (≤4 mg/min furosemide).
Hyperuricemia (gout), hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemiaChronic metabolic effects to note in the outpatient setting.
Loop diuretics are sulfonamides — a true, severe sulfa allergy is the one time to reach for ethacrynic acid, the only non-sulfa loop diuretic.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend every morning

  • Daily weight (same scale, AM) and strict I/O — net negative is the goal until euvolemic.
  • Daily BMP + Mg²⁺ during active diuresis — replace K⁺/Mg²⁺, watch Cr trend.
  • Exam for decongestion: falling JVP, resolving rales/edema, improving orthopnea, weight down.
  • Transition to oral diuretic once near euvolemic and confirm stable ≥24 h before discharge.
Escalate

When to call the ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers from the floor

Escalate to ICU for any of: SBP <90 or MAP <65 with hypoperfusion, or needing pressors/inotropes · lactate >2 and rising · SpO₂ <90% or distress needing NIV/intubation · refractory flash pulmonary edema · sustained/malignant arrhythmia · need for invasive hemodynamic monitoring or a vasoactive drip · urine <0.5 mL/kg/h, rising Cr, altered mentation, or ischemic hepatitis. When in doubt, a "cold" patient not responding to diuresis belongs in a monitored bed.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness criteria + where they go

Discharge readiness (don't send them home too early — it's why they bounce back)

  • Euvolemia achieved (or near-optimal), congestion resolved
  • Transitioned to oral diuretic and stable ≥24 h
  • Renal function and electrolytes stable at/near baseline
  • No symptomatic hypotension/orthostasis; SBP ≥90; rate controlled
  • GDMT initiated/optimized and documented; oral regimen tolerated
  • Education done (daily weights, Na/fluid limits, med adherence, when to call) and 7-day follow-up arranged

Disposition options — match intensity of need to setting

Home

Stable, euvolemic, manages own meds/ADLs, reliable follow-up.

Home health

Home + skilled nursing/PT/OT visits (IV meds, teaching, wound care, intermittent therapy).

SNF (skilled nursing)

Needs subacute nursing/rehab <3 h/day. Medicare covers up to 100 days after a qualifying 3-day inpatient stay.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Good rehab potential; can tolerate ~3 h therapy/day, ≥5 days/wk, needs ≥2 disciplines, physician oversight.

LTAC

Prolonged hospital-level care (vent weaning, complex wounds, prolonged inotrope) — avg LOS >25 days.

Palliative / hospice

Advanced (Stage D) HF, refractory symptoms, recurrent admissions; hospice = prognosis ≤6 mo, comfort-directed.
SNF vs acute rehab (IRF) hinges on therapy tolerance: IRF requires the patient to do ~3 hours of therapy a day across ≥2 disciplines. A deconditioned HF patient who can only manage short sessions goes to a SNF. Early 7-day follow-up + STRONG-HF rapid uptitration + cardiac rehab referral is the readmission-prevention trifecta.

🫀 ICU — cardiogenic shock, organ support & the drips
Admit

Cardiogenic shock — recognize & stage

🚨

Definition & SCAI SHOCK stages

Cardiogenic shock = SBP <90 for ≥30 min (or needing pressors/inotropes to maintain ≥90) plus end-organ hypoperfusion (lactate >2, urine <30 mL/h, cool/mottled, altered mentation) with adequate/elevated filling pressures. Hemodynamically: cardiac index <2.2, PCWP >15. Cardiac power output <0.6 W predicts mortality.

StageNameBedside picture
AAt riskLarge MI or acute-on-chronic HF; no hypotension/hypoperfusion.
BBeginningHypotension (SBP <90 / MAP <60) or tachycardia, without hypoperfusion; lactate <2.
CClassicHypoperfusion needing intervention (inotrope/pressor/MCS) beyond volume; lactate ≥2, ↑Cr, cool/mottled.
DDeterioratingFailing to stabilize despite initial intensification — escalating support.
EExtremisCirculatory collapse / refractory hypotension / arrest, CPR, pH ≤7.2, lactate ≥8.
Cardiac arrest is a modifier at any stage. Observed mortality climbs steeply C→E (~22% → ~70%). Staging isn't academic — it triages who needs aggressive escalation now.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines & what to trend

  • Arterial line for continuous BP in shock / on vasoactives.
  • Central venous access for vasopressors/inotropes and central labs (ScvO₂, lactate clearance).
  • PA (Swan-Ganz) catheter — not routine, but reasonable (Class 2a) in cardiogenic shock with unclear or mixed volume/perfusion status, to guide inotrope/pressor/MCS decisions and for transplant/LVAD evaluation. Classic CS pattern: ↑PCWP, ↓CI, ↑SVR.
  • Trend: lactate (clearance = resuscitation working), urine output, MAP ≥65, mentation, extremity perfusion.
Support

Pressors & inotropes

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Split the problem into two questions: Is the pressure too low (need vasoconstriction)? Is the output too low (need inotropy)? Cardiogenic shock usually needs both — a pressor to protect coronary/organ perfusion and an inotrope to move blood forward.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDoseEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 >> β10.05–0.5+ mcg/kg/min↑↑SVR, modest ↑contractilityFirst-line pressor in cardiogenic shock (SOAP II)
Dobutamineβ1 >> β22.5–20 mcg/kg/min↑↑contractility, mild vasodilation (may ↓BP)First-line inotrope for low output when BP tolerates it
MilrinonePDE-3 inhibitor → ↑cAMP ("inodilator")0.125–0.75 mcg/kg/min↑contractility + pulmonary & systemic vasodilationPreferred inotrope when on chronic β-blocker (bypasses the blocked β-receptor) or with RV failure / pulmonary HTN; renally cleared — reduce in renal dysfunction; more hypotension
Epinephrineβ1/β2/α (potent)0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑↑contractility + ↑SVRRefractory shock only — ↑lactate, ↑arrhythmia, worse outcomes as first-line
VasopressinV1 (non-adrenergic vasoconstriction)0.03 U/min (fixed)↑SVR, spares pulmonary vasculatureAdjunct to norepinephrine; useful with a vasodilatory component / pulmonary HTN
DopamineDose-dependent DA→β1→α5–20 mcg/kg/minMixedAvoid — more arrhythmia and worse CS mortality vs norepinephrine (SOAP II)
Match the receptor to the deficit: low pressure → α1 (norepinephrine); low output → β1/PDE-3 (dobutamine/milrinone).
Milrinone vs dobutamine (DOREMI showed no outcome difference — individualize): pick milrinone if the patient is on a chronic β-blocker (PDE-3 bypasses the blocked receptor) or has RV failure / pulmonary HTN; pick dobutamine if renal function is poor (milrinone is renally cleared) or you want a shorter half-life and less hypotension.
Airway

Respiratory support & ventilator

🌬️

NIV first, then intubate — and the initial settings

Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP) is first-line for cardiogenic pulmonary edema in the awake, cooperative patient. Positive intrathoracic pressure recruits flooded alveoli and reduces preload and afterload — a hemodynamic bonus in HF. It rapidly improves dyspnea and work of breathing and cuts the intubation rate (3CPO: strong physiologic/symptom benefit, no clear mortality change). Start CPAP 5–10 cmH₂O; use BiPAP if hypercapnic (PaCO₂ >45).

Intubate if: NIV fails or is contraindicated, obtundation / can't protect the airway, worsening hypercapnia/acidosis, refractory hypoxemia, or cardiac arrest.

Initial vent settings (post-intubation, cardiogenic pulmonary edema)

Mode
AC / Volume
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6–8 mL/kg
IBW — lung-protective
PEEP
5–10
unloads LV; titrate to O₂
FiO₂
100% → wean
SpO₂ ≥92%
Rate
14–18
match minute ventilation
Peri-intubation is the danger zone in shock: sedation/induction + positive-pressure ventilation can drop preload and BP abruptly. Have vasopressors ready at the bedside, use a hemodynamically stable induction agent (etomidate or ketamine), and avoid excessive PEEP in RV-failure/preload-dependent states.

Mechanical circulatory support

⚙️

When drugs aren't enough

DeviceEvidenceBottom line
IABP (intra-aortic balloon pump)IABP-SHOCK II — no mortality benefit in AMI-CSClass III — not routine.
Impella (microaxial flow pump)DanGer Shock (2024): 45.8% vs 58.5% mortality in STEMI-CS, NNT 8First MCS with a mortality benefit — but real bleeding/limb/renal complications; patient selection matters.
VA-ECMOECLS-SHOCK / ECMO-CS: no benefit with routine early useReserve for refractory shock / bridge at experienced centers.
Downgrade

When to step down & goals of care

⬇️

De-escalation criteria

  • Vasoactives: off pressors/inotropes — or on a single low, stable, weaning dose — for ≥6–12 h with MAP ≥65 off escalation.
  • Perfusion: lactate normalized/clearing, urine ≥0.5 mL/kg/h, warm and mentating, Cr stable/improving.
  • Respiratory: extubated and stable for several hours (or off NIV) on ≤ nasal cannula / modest FiO₂, with normal RR and work of breathing.
  • Rhythm & access: arrhythmia controlled, no active titration of a vasoactive drip, transitioned to an oral or stable IV HF regimen.
  • Not yet if: still needing frequent drip titration, borderline/relapsing perfusion, escalating O₂ needs, or an unstable rhythm — a premature downgrade just bounces back.
ICU disposition for the patient who can't be weaned off support: consider LTAC for prolonged vent/inotrope needs, advanced-HF evaluation (transplant/LVAD) for the right candidate, and an honest goals-of-care conversation / palliative referral for refractory Stage D disease.
